definition: A post-hoc calibration method that divides a model's logits by a single learned scalar temperature, softening or sharpening the predicted probabilities without changing which class is predicted.
details: Modern deep networks are often miscalibrated: they have become more accurate over time while their confidence has become less trustworthy, so a prediction made with 90% confidence may be right far less often. Temperature scaling, introduced by Guo and colleagues in their study of calibration in modern neural networks, fits one parameter T on a held-out validation set and rescales the logits by 1/T before the softmax. Because the transformation is monotonic, the predicted class and the accuracy are untouched - only the confidence changes. It is the simplest member of the vector and matrix scaling family, and it is remarkably effective: a single parameter often outperforms more elaborate methods on large vision and language models. Its appeal in practice is that it needs no retraining and can be applied to a frozen model, making it a standard step when a confidence score will be consumed by downstream code or compared against a threshold.

citation.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
